steps.title: Two parts to every stop
steps.body: Your overall stopping distance is your thinking distance plus your braking distance.

question.prompt: Overall stopping distance is made of…

options.text: The length of your car plus the road ahead

question.explanation: You travel during your reaction time too — overall = thinking + braking distance.

steps.title: What stopping is made of
steps.prompt: Put your stop in the order it happens:

items.text: Thinking distance — you react, the car keeps moving
Braking distance — the brakes slow the car to a stop

steps.explanation: Overall stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

steps.title: The two-second rule
steps.body: On dry roads, leave at least a two-second gap to the vehicle in front.

question.prompt: On a dry road, the minimum safe gap to the car ahead is…
question.explanation: Dry roads: at least two seconds behind the vehicle in front.

a.label: Wet road
a.body: Stopping distances at least double — leave a gap of at least four seconds.

b.label: Ice or packed snow
b.body: Stopping distances can be ten times the dry distance.

question.prompt: In the wet, your gap to the car in front should be at least…

options.text: Two seconds — the same as dry

question.explanation: Wet roads at least double stopping distances — leave at least four seconds.

steps.title: Know your distances
steps.body: Typical overall stopping distances: about 23 m at 30 mph, 53 m at 50 mph, 96 m at 70 mph.

question.prompt: The typical overall stopping distance at 70 mph is about…
question.explanation: At 70 mph you need about 96 m — far more than double the 30 mph distance.

steps.scene: On a main road, the car behind is tailgating you — far too close for comfort.

options.text: Ease off gently and increase your gap to the vehicle ahead
Brake hard to warn them off
Speed up to pull away from them

question.explanation: Ease back: a bigger gap ahead gives you and the tailgater room to stop safely.

steps.wrongBelief: If the car in front brakes suddenly, you can always react instantly.

options.text: You keep moving during your thinking time, before the brakes even start
Modern brakes remove the need for any gap
It isn't wrong — reactions are instant

question.explanation: Thinking distance exists because you travel on while you react — then braking begins.

steps.repairNote: No one reacts instantly. Your car covers ground during thinking time, then needs braking distance on top.

questions.explanation: Both parts count: you move while thinking, then while braking.

questions.prompt: On a dry road you should stay at least how far behind the car in front?
questions.explanation: The two-second rule is the minimum gap on dry roads.

options.text: At least double the dry distance
The same as on a dry road

questions.explanation: Wet roads at least double stopping distances — leave at least four seconds.

questions.prompt: The typical overall stopping distance at 30 mph is about…
questions.explanation: About 23 m at 30 mph; 53 m at 50 mph; 96 m at 70 mph.

questions.prompt: If you are being tailgated, you should…

options.text: Ease back to increase your gap to the vehicle ahead
Brake sharply to warn the driver behind
Match the speed of the car behind

questions.explanation: A bigger gap ahead protects both of you — never brake to punish a tailgater.
